speechtext:

The house resumed from Wednesday, May 30, consideration in committee of Bill No. 64, respecting dominion companies-Mr. Cahan -Mr. Gagnon in the chair.
On section 14-Incidental and ancillary powers.

After considering the suggestion made by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher), we have decided to strike out from paragraph (q) the words " the payment of dividends, or." This amendment will comply completely with his suggestion and I suggest that the hon. member move accordingly.

I move accordingly.
I should like to express my appreciation of the action of the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) in this regard.
The arguments of the hon. member were quite convincing, and, as he suggests, these powers may be inserted in special letters patent if they are found necessary.
Amendment agreed to.
There is another amendment to be made to paragraph (f), to insert the words " government or " after the word " such " in the thirteenth line. These words were omitted in the printing.
I move accordingly.

Amendment agreed to.

Dominion Companies Act
There is another amendment to paragraph (k), to delete the word "to" at the end of line fifty and insert a comma after the word " person " in line fifty-one.
I move accordingly.
Amendment agreed to.
There is another amendment to paragraph (k). The words "to any company " in line two on page 10 should read " to any other company."
I move accordingly.
Amendment agreed to.

There is an amendment to paragraph (u), that the same be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
(u) to distribute among the shareholders of the company in kind, specie or otherwise, any property or assets of the company including any proceeds of the sale or disposal of any property of the company and in particular any shares, debentures, or other securities of or in any other company belonging to the company, or of which it may have power to dispose; provided either that such distribution is made for the purpose of enabling the company to surrender its charter under the provisions of this act, or that such distribution, apart from the provisions of this paragraph, would have been lawful if made in cash.
This is practically the same as the present law, whereby a company in surrendering its charter and making a distribution of its assets may make that distribution of assets as such or in cash.
I move accordingly.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 18-Contracts of agent binding on company.

I spent some time to-day examining this provision and have had the advantage of consulting with counsel. I have decided that subsection 1 of this section should be amended in accordance with the suggestion made yesterday by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). I am sending a copy of this amendment to the hon. gentleman and perhaps he will move it.

I move that section 18 be amended by striking out subsection 1 and inserting the following in substitution therefor:
(1) Every contract, agreement, engagement or bargain made, and every bill of exchange drawn, accepted or endorsed, and every promissory note and cheque made, drawn or endorsed on behalf of the company, by any
agent, officer or servant of the company, within the apparent scope of his authority as such agent, officer or servant, shall be binding upon the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I notice this amendment contains the words "within the apparent scope of his authority," and for my own information I should like to know if that is the proper word to use. I understand the general custom is to use the words "general scope."
I used the word "general" yesterday and then corrected myself. I have not looked up the decisions but I feel quite satisfied that "apparent" is the proper word.
I submitted it to counsel this morning and apparently this is in accord with the English decisions.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 48-By-law for subdivision, reduction, increase, etc., of share capital.

I would direct the attention of the committee to paragraph (d) which reads as follows:
(d) change all or any of its previously authorized shares with par value, issued or unissued, into the same or a different number of shares of any class or classes without par value and' not having priority as to capital or being subject to redemption;
This paragraph should be read with the first part of subsection 1, which reads:
(1) Subject to confirmation by supplementary letters patent, a company may from time to time by by-law ...
(d) change all or any of its previously authorized shares with par value, issued or unissued, into the same or a different number of shares of any class or classes without par value and not having priority as to capital or being subject to redemption;
It should also be read in conjunction with subsection 2:
No such by-law shall take effect until it is sanctioned by at least two-thirds of the votes of the holders of each class of shares thereby dealt with, cast at a special general meeting of shareholders called for the purpose and confirmed by supplementary letters patent.
This I notice is an innovation; the same provision apparently is not found in the sections which this section replaces, that is to say, sections 58, 59 and 60 of the present act. I am afraid it is fraught with danger. There are features that I personally do not like and I am going to move later on that subsection (d) be struck out. My reason for asking that it be deleted may be found in the case I referred to when speaking early in February, or perhaps later, on the subject
Dominion Companies Act

of company promotions in general. I will not refer by name to the company in regard to which I am about to speak; I will simply say that a certain company in western Canada during the past few months has made a change in its capital organization. This is the story. In the early history of the company certain shareholders bought 4,500 preferred shares at $100 par value. At the same time 3,000 shares of common stock were sold at $100 a share. The preferred stock became entitled to voting power after one year's default in the payment of dividends. In 1933, dividends were not paid and very naturally the holders of the preferred shares concluded that they had a right to step in, use their voting power and take possession of the company. What really happened was this. In the meantime the holders of the 3,000 common shares had passed a by-law to the effect that these 3,000 common shares of $100 par should be changed to 15,000 no par shares. When the petition was presented to the appropriate authority-
Is that a dominion company?

No. I said so in my
previous speech on the subject, but I see the same danger in this subsection. When these holders of the preferred shares, because their dividends were in default, assumed that by reason of their voting power they could take control of the company, they with 4,500 shares, were met by 15,000 shares of no par value. This apparently had been done perfectly legally. The petition presented to the proper authority had stated frankly that the dividends were not in arrears, and in fact they were not when the petition was presented; apparently everything was in order. But this is what really happened. Those men who had paid out their good money, no less a sum than $450,000, found that that money had no voting power and they were left without the relief which they had every right to expect when they purchased those shares.
I am afraid that under this subsection the same thing could happen again, and in the case of a company in a similar situation, the preferred shareholders having no vote until their dividends were in default, the holders of common stock having voting power might meet and pass a by-law and appeal to the Secretary of State for supplementary letters patent, and apparently there would be no reason why they should not be granted; because, so far as I can understand, it is not necessary to consult the preferred shareholders in such a case. The only shareholders
[Mr Butcher.]
whom it is necessary to consult are those who have votes with respect to the class of shares " thereby dealt with."
The hon. member is entirely in error in that.

I shall be pleased to
have the minister show me wherein I am in error.

The hon. gentleman has
referred to a company which I understand was not under the jurisdiction of the Companies Act of Canada, and I can only assure him that if such a proposition had come before the Secretary of State during the past four years it would not have received approval. This clause is designed to prevent just such action as that to which he has referred, by providing, first, that in the case of these several transactions which are now being carried out frequently in the present days of depression and reorganization, they shall not be carried out except by the sanction of at least two-thirds of the votes of each class of shares thereby dealt with. Now whether or not the preferred shareholders have votes under the by-laws of the company, under this express enactment two-thirds of the shares affected must vote in favour of the reconstruction or reorganization proposed, and the votes must be cast at a special general meeting of shareholders held for that purpose, of which they have due notice. Moreover, as a further protection, even if the by-law is passed, even if each class of shareholders affected approve and confirm the proposed reorganization by a two-thirds vote of each class, then the whole matter comes before the Secretary of State, and the proposed reconstruction cannot be carried into effect except by the grant of supplementary letters patent. I cannot conceive of any other protective measures which I could throw about such proposed reconstruction,

Would not the Secretary
of State feel safer if the words " dealt with " were changed?
"Thereby affected."
Yes, thereby affected.

I am prepared to accept
that.

That is used in section
144.

Will the hon. member move that amendment?

Dominion Companies Act

I notice that the
Secretary of State used the word " affected," and if that word were here I should be satisfied. I am pleased to move therefore that the words " dealt with " be struck out and the word " affected " be substituted therefor after the word " thereby."

I suggest that there will be some difficulty if you make that substitution. There is this difference: "shares dealt with" means the shares referred to in the subclause; "shares affected" might be other shares that might be affected. The change suggested is a dangerous one. The subclause had better be left alone.

I think the words "dealt with" are really more specific; in my statement I used the word "affected," but there has to be the vote of two-thirds of the shares dealt with in the reorganization. I would like to meet the hon. gentleman's wishes.
It might read "of such shares," but I think the subclause is all right as it stands.

In the case I mentioned, which shares would the Secretary of State say were being dealt with-the common stock or the preferred shares? I would submit in the case I mentioned the preferred shares are not dealt with but they are affected.

They were certainly dealt with in the reorganization of the company. The hon. member was complaining that although the preferred shares were dealt with, the preferred shareholders did not have a vote. All I say to the hon. gentleman is this, that in drafting legislation each draftsman prefers his own words as he is accustomed to use them and it is very difficult to find words which are acceptable to all parties. I think on reflection the words "dealt with" are probably well selected. I am not obstinate about this matter; I am subject to the approval of hon. members of the legal profession but their real safeguard in this is that no scheme of that kind can get through unless it is authorized by a by-law which has been confirmed by the vote of two-thirds majority of each class of shares thereby dealt with. I think "dealt with" is the proper term because there may be classes of shares which are not dealt with and the holders of which have therefor no interest in attending a special general meeting for the purpose of confirming the by-law. I prefer the words "dealt with," but I am in the judgment of the committee.

Would the minister tell us what is the practice of his department in just such a case as has been set forth by my hon. friend opposite? If voting power is not given to the preferred shareholders until a certain contingency arises in the way of passed dividends and if before that happens an application of the common shareholders comes before the department for an increase in the number of shares or a subdivision of them, would the department consider the application of the shareholders who have the right to vote?

The object of this clause is this: although the by-laws of the company provide that preferred shareholders shall vote only in certain contingencies, and although this may not be one of the contingencies under which they would ordinarily vote, I wish to provide in this clause that they shall have a vote for this particular confirmation, and that if two-thirds of them do not vote for this particular purpose, then the Secretary of State would not even consider their petition. as after all that is done, they have to petition for supplementary letters patent when the whole matter must be reviewed by the Secretary of State before such supplementary letters patent are granted.

Would it meet the objection to insert the word "such" before the word "shares" so that the subclause would read:
Of each class of such shares.
I think the word "such" would cover it.
Perhaps the hon. member for Last Mountain will withdraw his last amendment.

Just a moment. I was going to ask the Secretary of State: Can it be said that in the case I mentioned the preferred shares are being dealt with? They are affected but in my opinion they are not dealt with; the only shares that are dealt with are the common shares. Could the matter be handled in this way-"thereby dealt with or affected"?

I do not keep in mind the particular case referred to by the hon. gentleman and I do not think I should be asked to give an opinion as to the effect of a reconstruction under another companies act with which I am not familiar and one which has not come to my attention.
Dominion Companies Act

I would
like to make an observation. Anything that will be detrimental to the reorganization of companies now in difficulties and undergoing reorganization, short of providing against fraud and that sort of thing, ought not to be imposed in this clause. That is a sound principle. Parties engaged in reorganization of companies have to meet very difficult situations; they weigh the balance of equity as between different classes of shareholders and they make the best proposal that can be put forward having regard to all interests. If you impose too many obstacles, you just make the burden that much greater in the effort to put a company back on its feet. If the provision is for another purpose, for preventing manipulation of shares for gain, that is a horse of another colour.

It seems to me that in this clause provision is made against what happened in the case to which the hon. member for Last Mountain referred. In that particular case 3,000 shares of common stock of a par value of S100 each were changed into 15,000 shares of no par value. The original incorporation of the company called for 4,500 preferred shares of S100 each with a provision that when dividends on the preferred stock became in arrears for one year the preferred shareholders then had a vote in the management of the affairs of the company.
Is that preferred or common stock?

There were 4,500 shares of preferred stock and 3,000 shares of common stock of a par value of $100 each. That meant that the preferred shareholders had $450,000 and the common stockholders had $300,000 in the company. The provision was that whenever dividends on the preferred stock were in arrears for a period of one year the preferred shareholders obtained a vote in the company.

And the
voting strength.

Yes. In the last year apparently the common shareholders who had the management of the company saw that they were not going to be able to pay dividends on. the prefered stock and they then passed a by-law changing their 3,000 shares of common stock of a par value of $100 each into 15.000 shares of no par value. When the preferred shareholders stepped in and expected to take over the management of the company they found that they had only 4,500 votes as against 15,000.

But that is exactly what this clause is intended to preclude and prevent. We are saying by statute enacted by this parliament that that thing cannot be done except with the consent of two-thirds majority of the holders of the 4,500 preference shares.

The way this clause stands now, the only shares dealt with were the common shares. The preferred shareholders' dividends were not in arrears at the time this was done, so they had no say, their shares were not dealt with in any way, but they were most seriously affected.
They were affected in respect of voting power.

Would it not meet the hon. gentleman's difficulty if both terms were used, "dealt with, or affected"? In one case you are dealing with shares actually changed, and the other shares would be affected. "Dealt with or prejudicially affected."

I am in the hands of the committee, but I do not agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in his construction. Although the common shareholders may have had their votes increased I do not yet see how that prejudices the rights of the preferred shareholders who had not the right to vote. Under the by-law they were given the right to vote in certain contingencies, but those contingencies had not arisen. I may be very stupid about it but I do not see how those preferred shareholders were affected, prejudicially or otherwise.

I think the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Both-well) made his point very plain. Three thou-, sand common shares, par value $100, were by virtue of a by-law passed in the ordinary way changed into 15,000 shares each having a vote. They multiplied the voting power of the common shareholders by five. I think it was a pretty sharp device to keep control of the company and prevent it falling into the hands of the preferred shareholders, so depriving the preferred shareholders of the rights contemplated when the fully paid preferred shares were set up and sold to the public.

I am not going to discuss the thing at length, but if the preferred shareholders took their stock on the clear understanding that they had no vote, I fail to see how, it matters to them, not having a vote, whether there were 15,000 votes in the common shareholders or 3,000. But I am willing to accept any suggestion in order to make progress.

Dominion Companies Act
I know my hon. friend is an excellent draftsman, and would like to use the same terms all through. Section 123 uses the word "affecting." Should not that word be used in both places?
I am quite willing to accept that. Section 123 does not use the words "dealt with."
The amendment moved by Mr. Butcher is that subsection (d) of section 48 be struck out.
That is withdrawn.
What is the next amendment?
"Dealt with or affected."

No, the next amendment
is to subsection 2, in the third line, which is the 39th line of the page. I accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) that we strike out the words "dealt with" and in lieu thereof insert the word " affected."

I am
opposed to that. I think we should keep both in, if we want to meet the situation visualized by the hon. member for Swift Current.

If this would be satisfactory to the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) I would move:
That the words "or affected" be added after the word "with" in the third line of that subsection.

I am perfectly willing to
accept that.

May I ask the hon. member for Swift Current whether he thinks that for the case he outlined he would find a remedy in the section as he proposes to have it? Were the preferred shareholders at that moment affected by the change? Not at all that I can see.
They had no voting power at all.
They might be potentially affected, but they were not actually at the moment.

I think they were. At the time they bought the stock they knew what the situation was. They said: If this company is not able to make its way, if it defaults in dividends for twelve months we are going to be able to take charge. They knew they were putting up most of the
money; I do not know all the details but part of this common stock went to the promoters. The preferred shareholders believed that when necessary they would get control of the company.
And they were not prevented by anything the hon. gentleman has said.

They were absolutely
prevented.
How?
Because they had only 4,500 votes as against 15,000.

But I state that in every
provision of that kind, where it is provided, as frequently it is, that in default of payment of dividends on the preferred stock the preferred shareholders shall have an exclusive right to vote, that exclusive right was preserved in that case, whether the common shareholders had 4,500 votes or 15,000.

This was not a case
of exclusive right, they were simply entitled to a vote.

Let me assure the hon.
member for Swift Current that I entirely approve of the position he desires to get into, I only question the means he adopts. I do not believe that adding the word "affected" will achieve the result he desires. I think the best proof of that is that the present occupant of the office says that it will not. If you had that kind of proposition advanced to the present occupant of the office the case would not be taken care of by having the words "dealt with" or "affected." I think you must make it stronger.
Is there an amendment?

The motion before the
committee, I understand, is that the words "or affected" should be added after "dealt with" in the 39th line of page 25. I am prepared to accept that.

If there
is any doubt, as suggested by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) I suggest that the clause be amended to read as follows:
No such by-law shall take effect until it is sanctioned by at least two-thirds of the votes of the holders of each class of shares thereby dealt with or which are or may be prejudicially affected. ...
That would surely cover it.

I think it is the same thing.

Dominion Companies Act

What the hon. gentlemen are doing, I tell them at once, is this. This subsection 2 relates to each and every of the preceding provisions. That is it affects (g), increase of the capital stock of the company, and so on. By this you are clearly tying lip the necessary operations of a company very materially. All that is provided so far in this section as drafted is that the by-law dealing with any class of shares must first have the approval of at least a majority of all the shareholders. This clause then provides that the class of shares dealt with must, at this, general meeting, also vote as a class, and by a two-thirds majority approve of the contemplated action. After that the Secretary of State must thoroughly investigate the matter before he issues supplementary letters patent. I think those provisions are sufficient; on reflection I quite agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury that the words "or affected" may cause a very great deal of trouble in the case of an increase or reduction of capital. I prefer to leave it as it is.

May I add one further word? I think the minister has settled the whole question. I think up to the moment it has escaped our attention that in the ordinary course this by-law must receive the approval of all classes of shareholders.
No.
The minister says that is the intention, but that the special class dealt with shall be represented by two-thirds of its number, so that you have the majority of all the shareholders-
There is nothing in the legislation which says that all shareholders must approve.
It is the shares thereby dealt with.
The by-law must first be passed.
The by-law is passed in the ordinary course.
And after the by-law is passed it must be sanctioned by two-thirds of each class dealt with.

It has been suggested that we are perhaps restricting and tying up the operations of a company. Hon. members will recall that in practically all the provisions with regard to preferred shares there is an express provision that the rights of the preferred
[M** ^eary.]
shareholders are not to be modified, altered, changed, amended, revised-every word a lawyer can think of is used-without a vote, generally, of three-quarters of the preferred shareholders. So it seems to me that it is not unreasonable here to ask for a two-thirds majority of those who, as I say, are "affected" or, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury says, are "prejudicially affected," which is perhaps a better expression. I certainly agree with the hon. member for York-Sunbury; I prefer his amendment to what has been suggested from this side.
It has been moved by Mr. Bothwell that subsection (2) be amended by adding the words "or affected" after the words "dealt with" in line 39.

I was suggesting-I have not gone through the formality of moving it-that instead of those words we add after the word "with" in line 39 the words "or which are or may be prejudicially affected." The reason I interpolate the words "or may be" is to cover the case brought up by the hon. member for Swift Current. There was no actual default in that case, and the voting power was not actually vested when this move was made. But that action was anticipated, and that was a pretty sharp trick, in anticipation of what was going to happen. While strictly speaking the shares might not have been prejudicially affected at the moment, undoubtedly there was a potential affection. I know it is impossible to provide for every case, but this may help.
So far as I am concerned I am quite agreeable to the suggestion made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, and I will withdraw my amendment in favour of his.

Then you simply throw
upon the Secretary of State the duty of investigating to see whether any other class of shares is prejudicially affected. That may be an impossible investigation in many cases, I should think.

It will not
change your position.

In regard to the suggestion
of the hon. member for Sbelburne-Yarmouth, the by-law must first be passed in the ordinary course, as he will admit, by a majority of the shareholders who have the right to vote.

Dominion Companies Act
Then, after having been passed, the by-law must be sanctioned by a vote of two-thirds of the majority of the holders of that class of share specially dealt with. All I can say to the hon. gentleman is that you cannot preclude all possibilities. If the proposition which he has suggested came before this present department of the Secretary of State it would have no chance at all-
Hear, hear.

I would prefer to have it
as it has been drafted, following consideration of nearly every aspect of the question, retaining the words " dealt with." If the committee is not favourable to that suggestion I would agree to " dealt with or affected." Then one can probably ascertain whether the other shares are affected at all, but the extent to which they are prejudicially affected is another matter.
Then do I understand that all amendments are withdrawn?

Under the circumstances I would urge the amendment I have suggested. It seems to me that with those words in the act, when a by-law is brought before the minister he will say to the applicants, " I think these shares are going to be affected, and you had better have that bylaw approved by those shareholders." It will strengthen the hands of the minister, so it seems to me advisable to include those words.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Explain.
Indian Act

This bill is to amend and consolidate the Excise Act. This act was consolidated in 1927 at the time of the general revision of the statutes, but the last actual revision took place in 1883. A departmental committee consisting of the commissioner of excise, the law clerk of the House of Commons, the departmental solicitor and the former chief inspector of excise has been engaged on this work for the past six months. This bill should not be contentious because in the main it consists of the consolidation of the act to include the various amendments passed since 1927. There is some rearrangement and reduction of sections as well as a simplification of language without essential change in meaning, and it is intended to facilitate the general administrative work of the department.

Hon. THOMAS G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 90, respecting the Caughnawaga Indian reserve and to amend the Indian Act.
Explain.

Under the terms of an order in council, P.C. 466, of March 5, 1889, the provisions of the Indian Advancement Act, chapter 44, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1886, were applied to the Iroquois Indians of Caughnawaga, in the province of Quebec, and for the purpose of giving effect to the application of the act, the reserve at Caughnawaga was designated "Caughnawaga Indian reserve" and divided into six sections.
On July 12, 1906, an order in council, P.C. 1419, in the purported exercise of the powers conferred by section 4 of the Indian Advancement Act, it was provided that the division of the Caughnawaga Indian reserve into sections be done away with, and that the said reserve be comprised in one section.
It now appears there was no provision of the Indian Act, or of any statute, authorizing

the making of the last mentioned order in council.
It is provided under the terms of this bill that all acts committed pursuant to the provisions of the order in council of July 12, 1906, P.C. 1419, be made valid and effective, and provision is also made for again dividing the reserve into six sections.
Is this legislation being brought down at the request of the people living on the reserve?

Perhaps the Postmaster General is familiar with the case which I have in mind. Some time ago a vacancy occurred in my own constituency. I am not complaining because this vacancy was created by the person who had been appointed being dismissed but I have serious complaint to make as to the way in which the vacancy was filled. I realize that to the victor belongs the spoils and I have no objection to a Conservative being appointed to a position when there is a vacancy.
If he is efficient.

That is one consideration. However, I do think that when these appointments are made some regard should be had for the kind of people appointed. As I said, a vacancy occurred in the district which I have the honour to represent in this house. When it became known who was to be appointed, protests were made by many individuals in Winnipeg. I protested against the appointment, I wrote to the Postmaster General but I got as much satisfaction from the department as I would have got if I had written to this desk. This man was not a returned man and I objected to his being appointed because he had a fairly long criminal record. However, he was appointed to handle His Majesty's mail and when I protested and kept on protesting, I got no satisfaction. A short time after this man was appointed his son came out of the penitentiary and he helped his father to handle the registered mail in the post office. I protested again and finally the post office was transferred from the father to the daughter as a means of evading the issue. Is this all the satisfaction a member of parliament can get from the department? I got in touch with

Supply-Post Office
35S5
the department on a question of policy but I could get no satisfaction. I actually went down to see the minister in his office, I made an appointment but I was unable to see him. I think it is a rather sad state of affairs when a man of this type is appointed to a position of this kind for purely political considerations. This man has been appointed to handle the mails and other valuables which go through the post office of a thickly populated district. To my own personal knowledge I know that many people in the district refuse to take their mail to this post office because of the record of the individual who has been appointed by the Postmaster General.
I regret very much that the hon. member could not see me at my office because every hon. member is welcome in my office when I am there.

Postmaster General is going to make to my complaint?

matter under consideration.

I complained in writing even before the appointment was made. I took it up with the officials w'ho were there and all that I have said can be confirmed. Yet I was unable to get anything in the way of satisfaction. It may be true that I am welcome in the office of the Postmaster General but I sat there for three-quarters of an hour and watched others going in and coming out while I was still waiting. I had given my name and stated that I wanted to see the Postmaster General on this particular question. This matter is a couple of years old now but this is the first chance I have had to raise it. I made an appointment with the Postmaster General for a certain time but I coidd not wait longer than three-quarters of an hour. Although this is in my own constituency I have no personal axe to grind. Possibly I may lose more than I may gain through creating antagonism in some of the individuals concerned. I think the main consideration in filling these vacancies should be efficiency and good character. I do not think the recommendation of a member of parliament should be taken into consideration. I would rather see the permanent officials of the government make these appointments. These appointments should be made purely on the basis of efficiency. At present they are just political footballs. When the Conservatives come into power they dismiss a large number of Liberals and a large number of Conservatives take their places; when the Liberals come into power I have no doubt
that they will replace a large number of Conservatives with a large number of Liberals.
Hear, hear.

That may be anticipation.
I do not think any hon. member viewing this matter apart from ordinary party prejudice would say that that is good for the public service. I think it is detrimental to the public service and I think it would be a good thing for the department and for hon. members if hon. members had nothing whatsoever to do with the nomination of men to fill vacancies. I am pointing out this case as an example of the vicious system of party patronage. I know how the appointment was made as I saw some of the files subsequently. It was made on the recommendation of the defeated Conservative candidate. I do not know why any candidate or any member of parliament should want to interfere in these appointments. I believe that by doing so he makes more enemies than friends, because when the appointment is to be made by patronage he may receive as many as ten requests for the position and he can satisfy only one. I should like to get an undertaking from the Postmaster General-I hope hon. members on both sides will support me in this-that these appointments to vacancies will be made without any flavour of partisanship and be based purely on merit. If I had anything to do with the administration of this department I would not fire a single postmaster unless he were inefficient and unable to perform his duties. So long as he was doing his task efficiently he would have the opportunity of staying in his position. There may be a change in government in twelve months or so and if that happens a number of these postmasters will know that, metaphorically speaking, their heads are going to be chopped off. The efficiency of the public service is impaired by such action. Could I have some understanding from the Postmaster General that he will consider my suggestion? I do not want him just to say that he will take it into consideration, as that statement is becoming too much of a byword. I should like to have from both sides of the house something in the way of a definite understanding that in future political patronage will not play such a large part in the filling of these vacancies.

This postmaster was removed and replaced by his daughter. There is no complaint against the new postmistress. I shall be pleased to make an appointment with the hon. member and discuss the matter with him if he will let me know when he wishes to see me.

The balance of the reduction is made up of smaller items. As I said before, Mr. Chairman, this reduction was made to the detriment of the public service. Let me point out a policy and principle which has been accepted by both sides of the house. In 1928, when I was in the position occupied by my friend opposite, it was pointed out that in the Post Office Department that year there was rather a heavy deficit. I undertook to justify that deficit by pointing out the necessity for the extension of the service, especially the air mail service; the need for new post offices and for the establishment of new public routes, and the fact that there were far flung sections of Canada that could not be reached except by air mail. At that time the expression of opinion on both sides of the house was to the effect that the Post Office Department was a department of public service. It was agreed that the department should give the best possible service to the people of Canada, that the better service given in the distribution of mail would add to the prosperity of the country. Deficits were not to be considered as serious. Of course it was understood that the minister and his officials would do the best they could to balance revenue and expenditure, but when the extension of service. throughout the country conflicted with the expenditure of public money the minister was not to be condemned for a deficit. That policy was accepted by the house. It was something of a pleasure to me to feel that I had the absolute support not only of the party to which I belonged, the government of the day, but of the 245 members of the house.
That policy has not been carried out. I understand as well as anyone does the need for economy, but I believe economy can be practised without crippling the service. When that economy results in a decreased service to

This surplus is particularly encouraging in view of the fact that the post office operates primarily for the purpose of serving the public, and is not expected to provide a surplus.

That statement has been proved to be correct. The revenue this year from the carriage of newspapers is $500,000 less than it was in 1932 before the increase came into effect. Why is that? This increase was put into effect in such a way that the newspapers figured that if it was paid they would have to throw the burden on the people and make the people pay an indirect tax through an increased price for their newspapers. Prior to that there was a special rate by express companies for the delivery of papers within certain distances- a limit of 300 miles-and they took advantage of that better rate by express to have their newspaper bundles delivered to news stands in the large cities, with the result that the Post Office Department lost that revenue. Further than that, within zones of twenty, thirty, or forty miles-someone says seventy-five miles-they delivered their bundles to various news stands in the small districts surrounding Montreal, Toronto, Kingston, Winnipeg and other places. These they delivered by motor truck.

I did not attempt to show that there was a different system adopted by the present Postmaster General from that which was adopted during my regime. If he thinks that, he has misunderstood me. I simply quoted the Minister of Finance; I do not know where he got his figures and I do not care where he got them; I quoted his statement and he made it plain in the house that last year in the Post Office Department there was a deficit between expenditures and revenues of more than $300,000. I leave the matter there. If the Postmaster General's report at the end of the fiscal year 1934-35 resembles the report he handed to me to-day, he will have to take the Minister of Finance

to task. I believe he is quite able to do so; he requires no help on my part to fight his own battles with the Minister of Finance and I leave the battle between the two of them.
It was not my intention from the very introduction of the Post Office estimates to go into any carping criticism of the department. It was not my intention to deal with my hon. friend as I was dealt with when I was Postmaster General and when I was taken along pretty rough roads in connection with the dismissal of postmasters and other matters which had a political aspect. I could if I wished place before this committee numerous instances where the Postmaster General of to-day is guilty of the very same things as those of which I was accused when I was Postmaster General. I do not blame him for catering to his friends if he will do it in a spirit of justice and fair play. I say to the present Postmaster General that when I occupied that position I catered to my friends and I was willing to take the responsibility, and if by the fortunes of war or of politics the Liberal party comes back into power within a short time and I am once more done the honour of being called into the cabinet as Postmaster General I shall play the same game as I played before.

That is
frank.

It is frank. Why should I criticize the Postmaster General to-day for the dismissal of eight or nine hundred postmasters, when if I become Postmaster General and my friends ask me to be as generous to them as the Postmaster General has been to his friends I could not do it after criticizing him. Therefore I do not criticize him; I congratulate him. He has set a pace for me if I ever get there again, and I will follow that pace.
Now, sir, having said that, and having been honest in my confession-they say open confession is good for the soul-

It is a dark outlook
for a lot of Conservatives.

-having said that much I wish to come now to a transaction of the department which I feel it my duty to condemn, and condemn very severely. I condemn this not because I want to put the blame on the minister, I am not attacking him personally, I am attacking what I consider or fear may be a policy adopted by that department with the consent and approval of the government, a policy that I would spurn and that I think will work to the detriment of the post office. It is the policy of giving out

Supply-Post Office
contracts without calling for public tender. I want to be fair; there are certain supplies required by the department for which there is no need to call for tenders. I can give instances; there is the stamp cancellation machine. The machine that the department is using in large part to-day is manufactured in Canada, the concern manufacturing it is the only concern that manufactures instruments of that kind in Canada. In the past we had to depend upon American machines, and we never could buy them outright, we had to take them under what is known as a lease contract, paying so much a year for the use, and in the end the sum became enormous. An effort was made to get a Canadian machine to replace them, and, in 1929, I think, such a machine was produced, and improvements have since been made so that today we have a Canadian cancellation machine that I think excels in speed, if not in absolute perfection, any American machine. That is to the credit of the inventive genius of our men in Canada. For a machine like that no tender can be asked, it is a matter of negotiation for the best price from the only concern that manufactures them.
Again there is no need to ask for tenders for typewriting machines of the standard in use to-day in the public offices of this country, because all makers of such machines have a standard price; no matter what company they are bought from the price is the same. Therefore the only thing that matters is to see that you give the order to the best man politically-speaking among the companies in that business. There is a certain lock for mail bags, there is no need of calling for tenders for that special style because it is sold at a standard price. And I could give other instances. I point out these in order to do full justice to the department. But I do condemn the idea and the practice of giving contracts for the manufacture of rural mail boxes without calling for tenders. It leaves in my mind the suspicion that there has been something behind the scenes in connection with the awarding of such contracts. In 1927, when I had the honour of being Postmaster General, we required a great many rural mail boxes. At that time the government accepted the policy that the department had recommended of extending as far as possible our rural mail routes, and in order to do so, having laid down a regular program which would take four or five years to carry out, we required a sufficient number of rural mail boxes to cover the period. I did not give nor sanction the giving of that contract without calling for tenders. We asked for tenders and received 47. We asked for designs, and
we received over 80 designs. These designs were all considered, as were the tenders, by a special departmental committee of experts in the work of mail delivery, presided over by myself. The minister himself did not decide who should get the contract. We proceeded by a system of elimination. The department itself had designed a rural mail box. We wished to do away with the old style boxes, at the request of the ministers of public works of many of the provinces, who pointed out to us that in view of the increasing automobile traffic on the highways the old boxes were dangerous because of the arms extending when the box was shoved out. We undertook to design a box that would be placed on top of the post with a swivel, so that in no position would it extend more than 7 or 8 inches beyond the post. We kept that design to ourselves. It was an invention of the department. At the same time word was given to those wishing to tender that we would prefer to do away with the arm style box, and asking them to submit something along the line of a swivel box or other improvement. They did so. By a process of elimination, after considering the matter for a couple of weeks, this committee brought it down to four designs, and four of the lowest tenderers, for swivel design boxes. Those designs were compared with our own and two out of the four came pretty close to the design invented by the expert in the department; and the contract was finally awarded on the swivel style basis. Some 35,000 or 40,000 boxes were ordered and we started in with the development of our large program for extended rural mail service. When I retired from the Post Office Department in August, 1930, there were 25,552 boxes on hand out of the large quantity we had ordered. But I find that as early as December, 1930, a contract was let for 10.000 rural mail boxes without calling for tenders. Further-and this is the part of the proceeding that I wish to condemn with all the force that I have-the information given on the floor of this house by the minister shows that these 10,000 boxes arranged for under that contract without calling for tenders are covered by a patent right. No box of that kind, accepted by the Post Office Department, has any right to a patent. The right lies in the government in the box we put into use in 1928, and the fact that the department has accepted the principle that the box shall be protected by a patent means that in the future that box alone shall be used in the rural service, and a monopoly is immediately created. That is the result of this system of giving out contracts without calling for tenders.
Supply-Post Office

Now let me proceed. I have notes here containing a great many figures, and I am going to follow my notes rather closely as I go along. I have stated that when the present government came into power they had 25,555 rural boxes still on hand. From August, 1930, to March 1, 1933, according to a statement submitted to parliament on March 8, 1933, only 5,546 boxes had been put into use, which would leave 20,000 of the 25,000 boxes still on hand, after a period of two and a half years.
How long would that supply last?

It would not last very long
if the service I started had been maintained.

As they had been given
out previously, how long would that balance on hand last?

I am coming to that; I
will develop it as I go along. In another . statement made by the minister in March, 1933, we find him saying that on December 22, 1931-about the time the order for ten thousand boxes was given-there were on hand 18,294 boxes. This would indicate that between September, 1930, and December, 1931, some 7,000 boxes had been used, but the former statement which I have quoted shows that only 5,546 boxes were put into use in the period from August, 1930, to March, 1933. I do not know where the discrepancy comes in, but that is the information that was given in this house. I ask the minister how he can reconcile these different figures. If the latter figure is correct the minister led the house astray-unwittingly, perhaps-when, on March 8, he stated that only 5,546 boxes had been put into use up to March, 1933. Therefore we had 25.555 boxes on hand in September, 1930, and an additional 10,000 boxes ordered in December, 1931, making a total of 35,555 boxes on hand or on order during the period between September, 1930, and December, 1931. The record shows that up to March 1, 1933, only 5,546 boxes were put into use. This would leave some 30,000 boxes still on hand. Even if no extra boxes had been purchased, using only 5,546 boxes up to March 1, 1933, it will be seen that 20,000 of the first lot of boxes would have been on hand as of that date.
In the light of these facts what becomes of the statement made by the minister, in an attempt to explain this order for 10,000 boxes, that the stock on hand was so low that an additional purchase had to be made? I do not wish to impute motives to the minister, but in the light of these facts I think I have the right to ask whether the purchase

was made to meet the demands of some hungry supporter, for it must be remembered that no tenders were called for and that the person who was given the contract was not a regular manufacturer but a retired commercial traveller who, I am informed, farmed out the work, on which he made a handsome profit.
The minister made several statements to the house in 1933, and some statements were made also by the acting minister in 1934. Let me refer to a third statement made in 1933. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) asked how many boxes were on hand as of January 1, 1931, 1932 and 1933 and also as of July 1, 1931 and 1932 and March 1, 1933. In . reply the minister said that in January, 1931, there were 25,000 boxes on hand; in July, 1931, there were 20,088; in January, 1932, there were 18,294 boxes and in July, 1932, there were 25,760 boxes. Evidently some of the new boxes had been received. In January, 1933, there were 25,638 boxes, and in March, 1933, there were 25,412 boxes bn hand. Now let me analyse this statement. I find that from January 1 to July 1, 1931, there were 2,912 boxes used. From July 1,
1931,	to January 1, 1932, there were 1,794 boxes used. From January, 1932, to July 1,
1932,	you will note that the number of boxes on hand increased to 25,760; it must have been about this time that the order for
10.000	boxes was being filled. Then from July, 1932, to January, 1933, only 122 boxes were used.
I am making this analysis to show that there was no need to buy the additional
10.000	boxes, especially when they were bought without tenders being called for. From January, 1933, to March, 1933, 226 boxes were used. In other words, according to this statement, from January 1, 1931, to March 1, 1933, a period of more than two years, 5,094 boxes were used. I am giving these three statements, which vary in each case. The committee will note that even in this statement the minister admits that there were 25,412 boxes on hand in March, 1933. According to one statement a calculation would show that there were 30,000 boxes on hand in March, 1933. I am not going to use that calculation; I will confine myself to the positive statement submitted by the minister in which it appears that 25,412 boxes were on hand at the end of March,
1933,	Accepting that figure as correct, for the sake of argument-and I have reason to doubt it, when I consider the previous statements referred to-I find that after placing 5,546 boxes in use from September, 1930, to March, 1933, more than 10,000 of the

Supply-Post Office
boxes on hand in September, 1930, would still remain. Again I ask what was the necessity for the purchase of 10,000 boxes?
Then I go on to develop the second feature of this contract which gives a patent right on these boxes to the person in whose name the contract was given. I shall not mention his name.
He is dead.

I understood that that
poor gentleman was dead. I can hardly blame him for dying under such conditions, I want to be fair. I do not wish to refer to the gentleman who got this contract or to give his name because, as the minister says, in the past few months he passed on to a better world. But I wish to condemn, and I do condemn with all the force at my command, the practice of awarding contracts for rural mail boxes without first calling for tenders. I ask the minister now to do away with the practice that has been established under his regime. If anybody has a regular, legal contract with the Post Office Department, for the manufacture of a box along the line that we designed in 1927-and I understand there is very little difference between that design and the patent design, although I have not seen it-the holder of the patent right can step in to-day and enter action for damages for infringement of patent against such contractor. That is what I fear. I fear that the carrying out of a practice of that kind will establish a monopoly, and once a monopoly is established the Lord knows where it will end. It is time to put a stop to it, and I ask the minister now if it is not possible to do away with that patent right.
No boxes have been purchased since December, 1931.
I know but-
The question was discussed at the last session.

But I was not here. I almost took the same journey as the gentleman that made the boxes, to the next world, and I was not in a condition to discuss the question at that time, but I am in a position to do so now, and that is the reason I am bringing it to the attention of the minister. I hope the minister will take what I have said in the spirit in which I have offered it. It is not a personal attack at all but a criticism of a practice that I fear is growing up in the department and which should not be 74726-228
tolerated. I think the minister has sufficient backbone and determination, when he sees that it might grow into an abuse to put his foot down and to say that in future things will be done in a more regular way.
Certainly, if someone suggests something irregular to me.
Item agreed to.
May I ask how many rural mail routes have been established in Saskatchewan in the last four years?
I will give that information to-morrow.
Not to-morrow. I presume the minister means Monday.
Perhaps to-night.
That is better, and will the minister at the same time give the number of mail routes established in the other provinces in Canada?
With great pleasure.

The figure of S657.000 is the surplus for the year ending March 31, 1933, but the minister submitted to me this afternoon a statement in answer to a question I asked him last night as to what was the revenue and expenditure for the year ending March 31, 1934, in which he showed that the total expenditure was $29,202,730.12, and the revenue $30,367,465.09, showing a surplus of $1,164,734.97 according to those figures.
Are the figures the former Postmaster General quoted for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1934?
Yes, those figures.

There are one or two more questions which I should like to ask. Would the Postmaster General state the amount of revenue received from the sale of excise stamps? I ask that question because there has been a change made so that now an ordinary postage stamp can be used on cheques where formerly an excise stamp was necessary. If we had the actual facts it might show the revenue of the post office in a somewhat different light. Can the minister

Private Bills

give to the committee the last available figures for the year prior to the change that was made allowing the ordinary postage stamp to be used on cheques? What was the amount of excise stamps sold in the last year prior to that change being made, and the amount of excise stamps sold since?
The tax on money orders for the year 1933-34 amounted to 8361,818.09, and the tax on postal notes 8143,712.67.

That is hardly giving the information I requested. Perhaps I may be given the information after the recess.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The house again in committee of supply, Mr. Gobeil in the chair.
Entomology, including investigations, and inspections relating to destructive insects and pests, $350,000.

Friday nights seem to be popular for grasshopper estimates, as I believe this is the third Friday night they

have been discussed. We should try to make this the last night. I recall that when discussing this vote last Friday the minister seemed to get huffed about something when asked a certain question. Well, we are not going to take scoldings from him to-night for replies, nor are we going to follow his example if we can avoid doing so. I want to ask him a question and I hope he will not try to imitate a fishwife in replying to me. I am referring to the grasshopper vote, or rather the grasshopper loan, and I want to state the situation as simply as possible to-night so that we or the minister shall not go off at a tangent. This particular loan is to be found at the top of page 360 of the votes and proceedings of May 23:
Order in council. P.C. 1051. dated 23rd May, 1934: authorizing loan of $1,500,000 to the province of Saskatchewan for the purpose of meeting commitments incurred or to be incurred in extending relief to farmers in the province by way of grasshopper control and by loans to the said farmers covering the seeding operations for the 1934 crop season, including the purchase of seed grain.
I emphasize particularly those words "grasshopper control." Now that is the only earmarked loan for grasshopper control I have been able to find. I do not think that I should be expected to have to hunt up all the orders in council to find all these loans made during the past four years to the prairie provinces. After a great deal of search this is the only one that I have been able to find which was made for the purpose of controlling grasshoppers and seed grain grants, in pursuance of the energetic campaign which I believe is still in progress there. In fact, I know that that campaign started last fall is still being waged. What I want to point out, however, is that the time to take weather precautions is not when the storm is on you; that is not the time to get your sails in shape, though I admit that it is better then than never. The time to have got ready was last year in the pre-hopper flight period. Vast flights of these pests darkened the sun at times, and with nothing to eat where they were, except just enough to enable them to grow into the stage where they could fly, they immediately sought pastures new in other parts of the province and affected large areas not previously affected. I congratulate the minister upon the fact that this year something is being done in a federal way. Both officers in front of him and especially the dominion entomologist, know that all that the dominion has ever done in the past until this year-there may have been something last year and I will therefore qualify the statement to that extent till the minister

Supply-Agriculture-Insect Pests
replies-has been to give expert advice and to oversee the campaign. There are a good many first class men in Saskatchewan and in the west generally doing that work but since there has been an entomological branch that has been the extent of their activities until this year. As I say, if the minister can assure us that there was some last year as well, that will go to qualify the general statement I make.
Now, does the minister know of any vote in any year, either during this administration or in any previous ones, or anything that has been earmarked like this loan for the purpose of grasshopper control? I do not think that I am flouting or taunting the government in askiqg that question; I do not think it is an offensive question. The question is a straight one and I should like to have it answered. I wish to know whether there are any other loans of this kind. If there are then they should be capable of being indicated without the discussion being diverted to something else about which I am not inquiring. I think I will give the minister an opportunity now to reply to that question because he may have an alibi; he may have another hopper control loan like this. These loans have been running for three or four years, and though I have not examined them all I examined them pretty well last year. If he will give us some information on this question that will throw some light upon it I shall be the first to congratulate him if it turns out that he did as the Americans did not only this year but last year, when they came to the relief of states affected and actually voted money for grasshopper control.

There is no difference in principle between what we have done this year and what has been done during the past two or three years. Last year at any rate money was advanced to Saskatchewan to enable them to carry on in the same way as ito the other provinces that presented the facts to us to show that they themselves could not finance their responsibilities as provincial governments. Last year money was sent, the same as this year, to assist in seeding operations, farm relief and other matters of that sort. The hon. member has himself been so long a member of governments that I am sure he will agree with me in this, that when a request is made for sums of money or for assistance the order in council is usually drafted using the phraseology of the request.
Last year we were asked by different provincial governments for assistance and money was loaned to the provincial governments: 74726-228J
and because it was loaned to them it was their money to use. They used the money we loaned them last year in purchasing poisoned bait for grasshoppers and in the carrying out of their campaign to combat the grasshopper menace. This year they were also assured, as they had previously been, that if they could not adequately finance the carrying out of what were their essential responsibilities they would similarly be given consideration and assistance.
As regards this money just being advanced, it has in no way affected the preparation for the campaign. Bran and bran substitutes have been bought as well as sawdust, poison and everything necessary in the way of equipment. Large commitments have been made, and this money so advanced has been used to meet these commitments. There has however arisen a difficulty as compared with last year, and it has been particularly aggravated during the past week or two, namely, the shortage of seed where the grasshopper menace is worst. This makes it impossible for the farmers to carry out a part of their campaign-the cultivation of land at the right time and in the right way in order to have as destructive an effect as possible on the grasshoppers.
The campaign this year has been organized much more thoroughly because of the greater menace over the three prairie provinces than a year ago. Reports were received from officials in charge of the campaign and also from those cooperating with them to the effect that the danger is all that had been forecast, even greater in some instances than could be imagined; and that has been made still worse by the fact that the conditions this year have been ideal for the grasshoppers to multiply to the greatest extent and, if not fought, to do the greatest possible damage. More than one thousand committees have been set up in Saskatchewan alone and the machinery with which they are working is and has been for some time going twenty-four hours a day, turning out this grasshopper bait. According to our latest report there is no lack of supplies or assistance, although it seems that more is needed than was estimated, because, as I have said, conditions have been so ideal for the grasshoppers to multiply. This year the young grasshoppers appeared from one to three weeks earlier than they did a year ago, and that has shown the necessity of the very careful planning that was done so that the whole machinery was ready to set in motion at any time. There are places where the stubble land was ploughed in the spring and not packed, where the grasshoppers are doing a lot of damage and destroying the crop to such an extent that the farmers feel there is

Supply-Agriculture-Insect Pests
little use in trying to save it and they are using those fields to distribute poison bait to keep the grasshoppers from the summer fallowed fields which so far have escaped any damage.

I hope I am not
too hard to satisfy in this matter. The minister has given us a very nice dissertation on the grasshopper situation in the west. He ought to know the conditions pretty well by this time because he has outlined them at least twice and he has done it well. I suppose practice will make him still better and the next time he outlines the situation he will do it the best of all. He has not, however, answered my question as to whether he can point to another earmarked vote like this in the history of Canada. His answer to this, if it were an answer, was that other loans were made and no doubt some of them might be and were used for grasshopper bait and so on. In that case the provinces did not observe the earmarkings; there was none. Does the minister mean to say that the Saskatchewan and other western governments get these loans and do what they like with them?
Let me indicate isome other earmarked votes. I would ask the minister whether he thinks the provinces could divert this to fighting grasshoppers or any purpose than that indicated:
Order in council P.C. 1046, dated 21st May, 1934: authorizing loans to be made from time to time to the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Alberta, not to exceed the sum of $750,000 to each province, for the purpose of assisting the said provinces to construct and maintain highways other than the trans-Canada highway.
That is an earmarked vote for a specific purpose just as this other hopper one is Does the minister really say that the provincial governments could divert that to hoppers or anything else? If they did that, they are very disobedient representatives.
I have another order in council:
Order in council P.C. 1022, dated 17th May. 1934: authorizing payment to the province of Saskatchewan of the sum of $10,324.54 for relief settlement.
When relief is required, surely they would not devote that relief, which I presume is for humans or perhaps animals, to feed grasshoppers even with poison. That explanation puts the provincial governments in the position of being very disobedient wards of this state. I recognize the fact that the federal government has been acting very generously to the provinces and the least they could do would be to observe the terms of the

loan. Therefore the minister's excuse involves disobedience on the part of the provinces and surely he does not want to put his friends, right at election time too, in that position. The minister will have to get up a better alibi than that, one that will not put his friends in wrong quite sc far. The more I listen to the minister's excuses and pleas the more I am convinced of the correctness of the ground I took two weeks ago that this was the first and only vote earmarked for grasshopper control ever given by any government.

Is the hon. member
objecting to it?

Surely to goodness
if I am wrong, some of the members of' the government should set me right when I am making these statements repeatedly and getting no answer. I can imagine what the minister said may have some accuracy in it; perhaps they did do that. In that case what is the position of the government? That they keep on giving, giving and giving indefinitely and then have no control over the money; the provinces can divert it to any purpose they like and in that case how much of it is diverted to election purposes?
Mr. 'BOWMAN:	Will the hon, gentleman permit a question?

I will remind my
hon. friend who is a lawyer that I am not in the witness box, but I will allow a question.
What proof has the hon. member that a single dollar of the money to which he is referring has been spent for election purposes?

I have not any proof at all; I was merely trying to show that if the government winked at disobedience on the part of the Anderson or any other western government and allowed them to divert a vote earmarked for one purpose to something else, there was no reason why they could not do the same thing for election purposes; they might start up a campaign against grasshoppers and have the country flooded with alleged grasshopper hunters. I am not drawing on my imagination; it is for the ministerial benches, including my hon. friend, to get some other excuses on behalf of the western governments. To state that there was any other vote than this one devoted to the destruction of grasshoppers is only proving disobedience that was not so marked on the part of the Saskatchewan government.
I am going to ask the question again, and I will include my good friend the hon. member

Supply-Agriculture-Insect Pests
for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) who is a very capable lawyer and an affable gentleman, although he is not called upon to answer; it is to the minister I am addressing my remarks because he has his officers in front of him, one of them being the chief entomologist. I do not know how long he has held that position, but it was long before my time. He is one of the most competent officers in the employ of the government. There is nothing he does not know about grasshoppers and all other pests of that nature. If the minister will just cuddle up to him a little bit, I am sure my hon. friend can get the information from him as to whether any other loan than this was given and earmarked for grasshopper control. Two weeks ago to-night the matter *was brought up in the house by the opposition including myself. Either the day after, which would be Saturday, or Monday, I cannot tell which, the thought struck the government it would be a good idea to earmark this million and a half loan for grasshopper control.
By the way, when the minister speaks again I wish he would tell me who made this recommendation to council. I do not think that is asking for any secret. The recommendation would naturally come from him, and from remarks made last Friday night by the minister and, I think, the Prime Minister, it was the Minister of Finance who recommended this loan to council. Well, it may be that that is right; the Minister of Finance having to do with loans and supervising the treasury-and I think he is doing it very acceptably

naturally it would be on his recommendation. But surely the minister would have the signature also of someone who knows something about the thing. The Minister of Finance will not mind my making that remark. He would expect to be advised by his colleagues the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Labour who has the administration of the Relief Act. It is quite a usual practice to have joint names on a recommendation of council; it may not be with this government, I do not know, but I know I had that experience many times in cases where two ministers were interested. May I ask the Minister of Agriculture if he "was a joint signer with the Minister of Finance of the recommendation to council on "which this order was based? If he can answer any of the questions at the same time that I have touched on, let him do so.

Mr. Chairman, I think I answered fully the point under discussion. When the different provincial governments cannot finance their obligations and when
they show just reason why they should receive assistance in meeting responsibilities that cannot be evaded, this government has loaned them money. A year ago loans were made to the governments for seed, for farm relief and matters of that kind, after submissions to us by the different provincial governments showing why they needed the money, and satisfying this government that their claims were just. There is no doubt that some of that money was used for this purpose, and property used. It was not a case of our not checking up on it; we checked up and satisfied ourselves that it was necessary for them to have it -before the money was loaned to them, but when it was loaned it was their money, and it was used for the purposes for which they asked it.
But they did -not ask for that, did they?

It was understood that that was one of the things they required money for. This year also requests were received, and assurances given earlier in the season that there would be assistance as far as necessary to enable them to carry out their responsibilities. It happens that in this case it was earmarked for grasshoppers, but as I told the committee the other evening the greater part of this money had already been spent. Commitments had been made, and our information at that time was that sufficient money had been advanced.

Well, I have made no progress yet in getting an answer. We have heard part of it three times now. The minister answered neither one question nor the other. For example, three weeks ago in the three prairie provinces there was every hope of a break in the series of drought years from which they have suffered. There was much more subsoil moisture than there had been for years, but during the last three weeks, and particularly during the last ten days, our reports indicate that conditions are worse than they ever have been. If three weeks ago we had asked any
province what amount they would require to carry on relief work for farmers and others, though they had given the matter their best judgment they could not have foreseen what was to happen, as a result of conditions over which no human agency has any control. Within the last week I had a letter from a friend of mine who drove through the south of Saskatchewan. He was forced to make detour after detour from the main highway because soil had drifted across the highway to a depth of from two to four feet. There are thousands and millions of acres with nothing growing on them. Live stock are starving for want of feed where they seemed to have good prospects for feed two or three weeks ago. Plans are being made already to shift the live stock to the north where there is feed; they realize that if this is not done immediately or if very heavy rains do not fall, they will lose all they have been hanging on to in the way of their homes into which they have put so much work.

There is another pest that we have in Saskatchewan and which I brought to the minister's attention last year. Information was sent out from his department about this pest, and I say that the information that was sent out was entirely wrong and caused our farmers the loss of hundreds of dollars last year. I saw many farms myself where the farmers lost hundreds of dollars through following the information sent out by the federal Department of Agriculture in reference to the cut worm.
The instructions given by the Department of Agriculture were that the farmers should not summer fallow until after the fifteenth of August, that if they did not touch their land until after the fifteenth of August a crust would form which would make it impossible for the moth to lay its eggs on the summer fallow, and that therefore there would be no cut worms the following year. I want to tell the minister that the farmers who followed those instructions, and I saw many who did, lost their seed, practically one hundred per cent of them, while those who did not follow those instructions but cultivated their summer fallow as in the past had no cut worms at all. Parts of a farm which had weeds were cultivated and those parts that were cultivated had no cut worms, while the parts that were not cultivated, following the instructions, had cut worms all over and the seed never came up.
The contention of the entomologists is that wherever the land is not touched. until after the fifteenth of August a crust will form and the moth will not be able to lay its eggs. But- the result actually is this: if a crust does form, when it dries up, cracks appear in it and the moth lays. its eggs in these cracks, and the cut worm is just as plentiful there as anywhere else. I know of farmers having quarter sections side by side. Those who followed the instructions of the department lost their seed, while those who did not follow the instructions but cultivated their land all the year had no cut worms at all. I draw this to the attention of the minister once more so that he may have his entomologists look into the matter, because the present instructions are costing many farmers all their seed, and they have to sow their seed all over again. That is true not only of one or two but of many, and they are generally our best farmers because it is our best farmers who take these pamphlets and try to follow the advice of the experts.
